back: Using existing knowledge and creating new knowledge to achieve the project's objectives and contribute to organizational learning.
Prior knowledge improves the outcome; new knowledge is collected for operations and future projects.
The key activities of knowledge management; integration brings together domain, contextual and project management knowledge.
Formal, systematic, codifiable in words, pictures or numbers. Easily shared through documents and systems.
Personal and embedded in a person's mind: skills, experience, insight. Hard to articulate; shared through conversation.
It lacks context and is open to different interpretations, so it is not always understood or applied correctly.

front: An important objective of knowledge management
back: Converting tacit knowledge into explicit knowledge when possible.
Decide early what to collect during the project and at closure; look at team assignments, the RBS, the stakeholder register and past lessons.

front: What shapes the choice of knowledge tools
back: The degree of innovation, project complexity, and the diversity of disciplines in the team.
Knowledge gained in a project, phase or iteration: situation, impacts, recommendations, proposed actions.

front: When is the lessons learned register created?
back: Early in the project, as an output of Manage Project Knowledge; then updated by many processes.
The persons or teams involved in the work, by any suitable means, including video, pictures or audio.
Where lessons from projects are kept for the organization; part of the organizational process assets.
A structured review of what happened, why, and how to do better; typically at the end or after significant milestones.
A structured review at various stages of the life cycle, not only at the end.
A retrospective is a frequent form of lessons learned meeting, at least every iteration.
Codifying lessons, the lessons learned register, library services, web searches, the PMIS. Best for simple, codified explicit knowledge.
Add interaction, such as a "contact me" link to the author of a lesson.
Networking, communities of practice, work shadowing, forums, events, workshops, knowledge fairs and cafés, interactive training.
A group (also called a community of interest) where people with a shared field exchange knowledge across projects.
Lessons and good practices told as narratives; particularly effective for tacit knowledge.

front: The most important part of knowledge management
back: An atmosphere of trust so people are motivated to share (Sixth Edition). Tools fail without it.

front: A trust-filled environment for tacit knowledge
back: Open communication, mentoring relationships, team building, face-to-face interaction, regular brainstorming.
Interview bots and other AI capture tacit and explicit knowledge; risks: leaking sensitive data, hallucinations. Use responsible AI policies.
Rotating roles so everyone drives and reviews work: knowledge gaps surface early and ownership is shared.
